summary: Defines an experimental ICMP message type for IPv4 used with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). It dynamically updates identifier and locator bindings for an existing ILNP session. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: ILNP separates a node's name from the addresses that reach it, so a node can have several addresses at once and change them without disturbing its conversations. RFC 6745 defines the message an IPv4 node sends when its addresses change. The message lists every address that is currently valid, each with a preference and a time limit, and every correspondent replies to say it arrived.

questions: how does ilnp update locators on ipv4
what is the ilnpv4 locator update message
how does ilnp handle node mobility
when should a node send a locator update advertisement
subtitle: An ICMP message that tells ILNP nodes when the addresses of a correspondent change.

tldr.problem: In ILNP for IPv4, a node may acquire new network addresses as it moves or multihomes, and its peers need to learn about them to keep sending packets to the right place.
tldr.mechanism: An ICMP message of type 253 carries the sender's currently valid locators, each with a preference and a validity period. Recipients can acknowledge receipt or update their routing information.
tldr.outcome: This is an experimental proposal that remains undeployed, as ILNP itself is experimental and has not been adopted by the Internet community.

facts.label: IANA request
facts.value: None; the type is shared experimental use

today: RFC 6745 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the IPv4 counterpart of RFC 6743 in the ILNP document set from the IRTF Routing Research Group. The memo makes no request of IANA: it notes that the ICMP type comes from the shared experimental range in RFC 4727, and that if the IETF were to standardise ILNPv4, allocating a unique type for the Locator Update would be the sensible thing to do.

sections.title: Why ILNPv4 Needs a Locator Update
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol is an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It separates a node's identifier, which is stable, from its locators, which are the addresses that reach it. A node may have several locators at once, and the set changes when the node moves, when it gains or loses a network connection, or when it multihomes.

ILNP has more than one possible engineering instantiation. ILNPv6 is the instance based on and backwards compatible with IPv6, and ILNPv4 the one based on IPv4. This document defines the new ICMP Locator Update message, used by an ILNPv4 node to inform its correspondent nodes of any change to its set of valid locators. It must only be used for ILNPv4 sessions, and authentication is always required. The memo notes that while the specification uses ICMP, on the grounds that this is a control message, there is no architectural difference between using ICMP and using some other framing, for example UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: ILNP gives a node a stable name and separate addresses that reach it. When those addresses change, the node has to tell the machines it is talking to, and this message is how the IPv4 version of ILNP does that.

sections.title: Where This Fits in the ILNP Set
sections.content:
The memo points at the other documents in the set for everything it does not cover. RFC 6740 is the main architectural description of ILNP, including the concept of operations. RFC 6741 covers the engineering and implementation considerations common to both ILNPv4 and ILNPv6, and RFC 6742 defines additional DNS resource records that support ILNP.

Two documents matter most for this message. RFC 6746 defines an IPv4 Nonce Option used by ILNPv4 nodes to carry a security nonce to prevent off-path attacks against ILNP ICMP messages, and also defines an IPv4 Identifier Option used by ILNPv4 nodes. RFC 6743 defines the matching message for IPv6, along with the IPv6 Nonce Destination Option in RFC 6744. RFC 6747 covers extensions to the Address Resolution Protocol for ILNPv4, and RFC 6748 describes optional deployment functions that are not needed to operate ILNP.
sections.plainLanguage: This message is one piece of a larger set. The architecture, the shared engineering rules and the DNS records live in their own documents, and the IPv4 options that carry the nonce and the identifier are defined separately.

sections.title: The ICMP Locator Update Message
sections.content:
The message has ICMP type 253 and code 0, and the checksum is calculated in the same way as for any other IPv4 ICMP message. The number of locators field gives how many 32-bit locator values are advertised. Each locator is followed by a 16-bit preference, which says how preferable it is relative to the other valid locators and uses the same syntax and meaning as the preference values for L32 records in RFC 6742, and a lifetime, which is the maximum number of seconds that particular locator may be considered valid, normally the same as the DNS lifetime of the corresponding L32 record.

The operation field says whether the message is a Locator Update Advertisement, with value 0x01, or a Locator Update Acknowledgement, with value 0x02. All other values are reserved for future revisions. The reserved field must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

The memo makes one point emphatically about the type number. The ICMP type value is allocated for shared experimental use in section 8 of RFC 4727 and is not uniquely assigned to ILNPv4, so implementations need to code particularly defensively, as other IPv4 experiments might be using the same type value for an entirely different purpose with a different packet format.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a short header followed by one block per address: the address itself, a number saying how much the sender prefers it, and how long it stays valid. Because the type number is shared with other experiments, a receiver has to be careful about what it accepts.

sections.title: Sending, Acknowledging and Storing the Update
sections.content:
A node whose set of valid locators has changed must send a Locator Update Advertisement to each correspondent node for each active unicast ILNP session. The receiver of a valid advertisement, meaning the authentication checks all passed and the advertisement came from a current correspondent, must send a Locator Update Acknowledgement back. The acknowledgement body is identical to the advertisement body except for the operation value.

Every ILNPv4 Locator Update message must contain a valid ILNPv4 Identifier Option and must contain an ILNPv4 Nonce Option. A node sending an update must include all currently valid locator values in the message, and a node receiving a valid update must replace the previously current set of locators for that correspondent in its own Identifier Locator Communication Cache with the newly received set. Every implementation needs to cope with a large number of locators in a single message, because a multihomed node or site might have many upstream links to different service providers, each with its own locator value.

To keep the incremental deployability and backwards compatibility that ILNP needs, the network layer needs a mode bit in the Transport Control Block, or its equivalent, to track which IP sessions use the classic IPv4 mode and which use ILNPv4 mode. The message has no impact on any transport protocol: it may affect where packets for a given transport-layer session are sent, but decoupling transport protocols and transport-layer session information from network-layer changes is an ILNP design objective.
sections.plainLanguage: The advertisement lists every address that currently works, not just the ones that changed, and the receiver replaces its whole list for that correspondent with what it receives. The receiver then says it has arrived, so the sender knows the change has landed.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
The message uses the same checksum calculation as any other IPv4 ICMP message, so a node that does not know the type can still check it and discard it.

When ILNPv4 is not in use, the receiving IPv4 mode must discard the Locator Update packet without processing it. That is what lets the protocol be deployed one node at a time. The implementation section adds that because the type uses an experimental value from RFC 4727, care should be taken when using it alongside other protocols that also use experimental values.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer that does not use this protocol simply throws the message away, so the message can be introduced gradually.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for the overall ILNP architecture are in RFC 6740 and the common ones in RFC 6741. The message must only be used for ILNPv4 sessions.

The ILNPv4 Nonce Option from RFC 6746 must be present in packets carrying the message, and the received nonce option must hold the correct nonce value for the packet to be accepted and passed on for processing. If either requirement is not met, the packet must be discarded as a forgery and a security event should be logged. Sessions in higher risk environments should use IP Security for ILNP in addition to the nonce option; using IPsec does not permit the packet to be sent without the nonce option, because the nonce lets a receiver do an inexpensive check before any costly cryptographic calculation.

Two further points are made. Implementations must cope with a message containing a large number of locator and preference values without developing a security fault such as a stack overflow. And if the nonce value is predictable, an off-path attacker might be able to forge data or control packets, a risk that is also mitigated by the common practice of IP source address filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: The message must carry a nonce that only the real sender could know, and a receiver that finds it wrong throws the packet away and logs it. The nonce is cheap to check, so it is checked before any expensive cryptography is done.

data.title: ILNPv4 Locator Update, header and first locator

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 253, taken from the shared experimental range.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: The ICMP checksum, calculated as for any other IPv4 ICMP message.

fields.name: Operation
fields.desc: 0x01 for an advertisement, 0x02 for an acknowledgement.

fields.name: RESERVED
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Locator
fields.desc: A 32-bit locator currently valid for the sending node. The block is repeated once per locator.

fields.name: Preference
fields.desc: How preferable this locator is relative to the others, as for L32 records.

fields.name: Lifetime
fields.desc: The maximum number of seconds this locator may be considered valid.

items.label: Locator Update Advertisement
items.desc: Sent by a node whose set of valid locators has changed.

items.label: Locator Update Acknowledgement
items.desc: Sent back by the receiver of a valid advertisement.

messages.label: Locator Update Advertisement
messages.note: The full set of currently valid locators, with a preference and lifetime for each.

messages.label: Locator Update Acknowledgement
messages.note: The same body, with the operation value changed.
